short_definition: Second-order thinking is considering not just the immediate result of a decision, but the consequences of those consequences over time, asking 'And then what?' before acting.
explanation: Second-order thinking goes past the obvious first effect of a decision. First-order thinking stops at 'This will save me money' or 'This will make customers happy.' Second-order thinking asks how other people will react, what the decision leads to in six months or five years, and what new problems it creates. One simple method is to list the likely effects of a decision at three time frames: 10 minutes, 10 months and 10 years.

Many choices that feel good now backfire later, and many that feel uncomfortable now pay off. Common examples are lifestyle upgrades that permanently raise fixed costs, discounts that teach customers to wait for sales, and skipping sleep to work more, then losing productivity.

The risk is analysis paralysis. You can't predict every knock-on effect, and over-thinking small, easily reversed decisions wastes time. Save deep second-order analysis for decisions that are expensive, long-lasting or hard to undo.
example: Example (illustrative numbers): you get a raise of 300 a month and are considering a car lease that costs 300 a month. First-order thinking says, 'I can afford it.' Second-order thinking notices that the lease locks in the cost for, say, 36 months (10,800 in total), that insurance may also rise, and that the raise no longer goes toward savings or paying down debt. With that in view, you might pick a cheaper option and put part of the raise into an emergency fund.
common_mistake: Stopping at the first, most obvious outcome. The opposite mistake is applying elaborate long-term analysis to small decisions that are easy to reverse.
title: Second-Order Thinking
